content: 1. Severe disease and mortality in patients with COVID-19 were analyzed through a meta-analysis published in BMC Public Health in 2021, volume 21, issue 1, article 1505. 2. Louie JC and Tapsell LC conducted a systematic review on the association between total sugar intake versus added sugar intake and diet quality, published in Nutrition Reviews in 2015, volume 73, issue 12, pages 837–857. 3. Te Morenga L, Mallard S, and Mann J performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials and cohort studies to investigate the relationship between dietary sugars and body weight, published in BMJ in 2012, article e7492. 4. Pan B et al. explored the association of soft drink and 100% fruit juice consumption with all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, and cancer mortality through a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies, published in Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition in 2022, volume 62, issue 32, pages 8908–8919. 5. The World Health Organization (WHO) published guidelines on sugar intake for adults and children, accessible via their website as of January 1, 2023. 6. Magnuson BA et al. reviewed the biological fate of low-calorie sweeteners, published in Nutrition Reviews in 2016, volume 74, issue 11, pages 670–689. 7. Ahmad R and Dalziel JE examined the role of G protein-coupled receptors in taste physiology and pharmacology, published in Frontiers in Pharmacology in 2020, article 587664. 8. Laffitte A, Neiers F, and Briand L discussed the functional roles of sweet taste receptors in oral and extraoral tissues, published in Current Opinion in Clinical Nutrition and Metabolic Care in 2014, volume 17, issue 4, pages 379–385. 9. Plaza-Diaz J et al. provided an update on recent studies regarding the plausible biological interactions of lowand non-calorie sweeteners with the intestinal microbiota, published in Nutrients in 2020, volume 12, issue 4, article 1153. 10. Hunter SR et al. highlighted the physiological effects of low-calorie sweeteners in humans, published in Nutrients in 2019, volume 11, issue 11, article 2717. 11. Rother KI, Conway EM, and Sylvetsky AC reviewed how non-nutritive sweeteners influence hormones and health, published in Trends in Endocrinology and Metabolism in 2018, volume 29, issue 7, pages 455–467. 12. Pepino MY investigated the metabolic effects of non-nutritive sweeteners, published in Physiology & Behavior in 2015, volume 152, part B, pages 450–455. 13. Burke MV and Small DM explored the physiological mechanisms by which non-nutritive sweeteners may impact body weight and metabolism, published in Physiology & Behavior in 2015, volume 152, part B, pages 381–388. 14. Russell C et al. analyzed global trends in added sugars and non-nutritive sweetener use in the packaged food supply, discussing drivers and implications for public health, published in Public Health Nutrition in 2022, pages 1–13. 15. Russell C et al. also reviewed the drivers, trends, and dietary impacts of non-nutritive sweeteners in the food supply, published in Nutrition Research Reviews in 2021, volume 34, issue 2, pages 185–208. 16. Popkin BM and Hawkes C examined the global sweetening of diets, particularly beverages, and discussed patterns, trends, and policy responses, published in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology in 2016, volume 4, issue 2, pages 174–186. 17. O BYS et al. studied the use of non-nutritive and low-calorie sweeteners in 19,915 local and imported pre-packaged foods in Hong Kong, published in Nutrients in 2021, volume 13, issue 6, article 1861. 18. Venegas Hargous C et al. investigated the consumption of non-nutritive sweeteners by preschoolers in Chile before the implementation of the Chilean food labeling and advertising law, published in Nutrition Journal in 2020, volume 19, issue 1, article 69. 19. González-Rodríguez M et al. assessed the presence and consumption of lowand no-calorie sweeteners among the Portuguese adult population, published in Nutrients in 2021, volume 13, issue 11, article 4186. 20. Martyn D et al. reviewed global intakes of low-/no-calorie sweeteners, published in Nutrients in 2018, volume 10, issue 3, article 357. 21. Nunn R et al. examined the prevalence and types of non-nutritive sweeteners in the New Zealand food supply in 2013 and 2019, published in Nutrients in 2021, volume 13, issue 9, article 3228. 22. Bolt-Evensen K et al. studied the consumption of sugar-sweetened and artificially sweetened beverages from childhood to adulthood in relation to socioeconomic status over 15 years in Norway, published in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity in 2018, volume 15, issue 1, article 8. 23. Hafner E and Pravst I reported a sharp rise in the use of lowand no-calorie sweeteners in non-alcoholic beverages in Slovenia based on 2020 data, published in Frontiers in Nutrition in 2021, article 778178. 24. Dunford EK et al. compared the types and amounts of non-nutritive sweeteners purchased by US households in 2002 and 2018 using Nielsen Homescan data, published in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics. 25. Sylvetsky AC et al. analyzed trends in low-calorie sweetener consumption among pregnant women in the United States, published in Current Developments in Nutrition in 2019, volume 3, issue 4, article nzz004. 26. Mosdøl A et al. reviewed hypotheses and evidence related to intense sweeteners and their effects on appetite and body weight changes, published in PLoS One in 2018, volume 13, issue 7, article e0199558. 27. Sylvetsky AC and Dietz WH discussed whether nutrient-content claims guide or confuse consumers, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2014, volume 371, issue 3, pages 195–198. 28. Dalenberg JR et al. demonstrated that short-term consumption of sucralose with carbohydrates impairs neural and metabolic sensitivity to sugar in humans, published in Cell Metabolism. 29. Fowler SP et al. investigated the long-term weight gain associated with artificially sweetened beverage use, published in Obesity (Silver Spring) in 2008, volume 16, issue 8, pages 1894–1900. 30. Chia CW et al. studied the risk of abdominal obesity among older adults associated with chronic low-calorie sweetener use, published in PLoS One in 2016, volume 11, issue 11, article e0167241. 31. Mattes RD and Popkin BM reviewed the effects of non-nutritive sweetener consumption on appetite and food intake, published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2009, volume 89, issue 1, pages 1–14. 32. Gaziano TA et al. highlighted the growing epidemic of coronary heart disease in lowand middle-income countries, published in Current Problems in Cardiology in 2010, volume 35, issue 2, pages 72–115. 33. Wekesah FM et al. explored perceptions and understanding of cardiovascular diseases and their risk factors among residents of urban informal settings in Nairobi, published in BMJ Open in 2019, volume 9, issue 6, article e026852. 34. Negesa LB et al. assessed patients’ knowledge of cardiovascular risk factors and associated lifestyle behaviors in Ethiopia in 2018, published in PLoS One in 2020, volume 15, issue 6, article e0234198. 35. Oli N et al. conducted in-depth interviews on the causes and prevention of cardiovascular disease among people with cardiometabolic conditions in peri-urban Nepal, published in Global Health Action in 2014, volume 7, article 24023. 36. Erhardt L and Hobbs FD surveyed public perceptions of cardiovascular risk in five European countries, published in the International Journal of Clinical Practice in 2002, volume 56, issue 9, pages 638–644. 37. Manafé M et al. examined South African adults’ views on their body weight and perceived risks of developing obesity and non-communicable diseases, published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health in 2021, volume 18, issue 21, article 11265. 38. Akindele MO et al. studied the relationship between body fat percentage and body mass index in overweight and obese individuals in an urban African setting, published in the Journal of Public Health in Africa in 2016, volume 7, issue 1, article 515. 39. Bosire EN et al. explored obesity normalization in urban-poor South Africa, published in Public Health Nutrition in 2020, volume 23, issue 9, pages 1515–1526. 40. Collins AA et al. investigated preferred body size among urban Ghanaian women and its implications for the overweight/obesity problem, published in the Pan African Medical Journal in 2016, volume 23, article 239. 41. Agyapong NAF et al. studied body weight, obesity perception, and actions to achieve desired weight among rural and urban Ghanaian adults, published in the Journal of Obesity in 2020, article 7103251. 42. Frayon S et al. reported on weight status misperception among Pacific adolescents aged 11–16 years in New Caledonia, published in BMC Public Health in 2017, volume 17, issue 1, article 25. 43. The Global Database on the Implementation of Nutrition Action (GINA) provides information on nutrition policies and actions, accessible via the WHO website as of January 1, 2023. 44. Food-based dietary guidelines are available on the FAO website, accessed in January 2023. 45. Sylvetsky AC et al. conducted a pilot study on parents’ perceptions of giving non-nutritive sweeteners to their children, published in the International Journal of Pediatrics in 2014, article 819872. 46. Williams P reviewed consumer understanding and use of health claims for foods, published in Nutrition Reviews in 2005, volume 63, issue 7, pages 256–264. 47. Hodgkins CE et al. examined how consumers categorize health-related claims on foods, published in Nutrients in 2019, volume 11, issue 3, article 539. 48. Wills JM et al. studied European consumers’ attitudes, understanding, and purchasing behavior regarding health claims, published in the Proceedings of the Nutrition Society in 2012, volume 71, issue 2, pages 229–236. 49. De Boer A reviewed 15 years of regulating nutrition and health claims in Europe, published in Nutrients in 2021, volume 13, issue 5, article 1725. 50. Van der Horst K et al. conducted a scoping review on consumer understanding, perception, and interpretation of serving size information on food labels, published in Nutrients in 2019, volume 11, issue 9, article 2189. 51. Allen L et al. reviewed the relationship between socioeconomic status and non-communicable disease behavioral risk factors in lowand lower-middle-income countries, published in The Lancet Global Health in 2017, volume 5, issue 3, pages e277–e289. 52. Dinsa GD et al. systematically reviewed the relationship between obesity and socioeconomic status in developing countries, published in Obesity Reviews in 2012, volume 13, issue 11, pages 1067–1079. 53. Vazquez CE and Cubbin C reviewed literature on socioeconomic status and childhood obesity to inform intervention research, published in Current Obesity Reports in 2020, volume 9, issue 4, pages 562–570. 54. Newton S et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the relationship between socioeconomic status over the life course and obesity, published in PLoS One in 2017, volume 12, issue 5, article e0177151. 55. Caro JC et al. evaluated the impact of Chile’s 2014 sugar-sweetened beverage tax on prices and purchases in an urban environment, published in PLoS Medicine in 2018, volume 15, issue 7, article e1002597. 56. Nakamura R et al. assessed the 2014 sugar-sweetened beverage tax in Chile through an observational study in urban areas, published in PLoS Medicine in 2018, volume 15, issue 7, article e1002596. 57. Lobstein T et al. reviewed the costs, equity, and acceptability of three policies to prevent obesity, published in Obesity Science & Practice in 2020, volume 6, issue 5, pages 562–583. 58. Frohlich KL and Potvin L discussed the inequality paradox in public health practice, published in the American Journal of Public Health in 2008, volume 98, issue 2, pages 216–221. 59. Wang YC et al. modeled the health and cost impacts of a penny-per-ounce tax on sugar-sweetened beverages, published in Health Affairs (Millwood) in 2012, volume 31, issue 1, pages 199–207. 60. Long MW et al. evaluated the cost-effectiveness of a sugar-sweetened beverage excise tax in the US, published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine in 2015, volume 49, issue 1, pages 112–123. 61. Lal A et al. modeled the health benefits of a sugar-sweetened beverage tax across different socioeconomic groups in Australia, published in PLoS Medicine in 2017, volume 14, issue 6, article e1002326. 62. Basto-Abreu A et al. assessed the cost-effectiveness of the sugar-sweetened beverage excise tax in Mexico, published in Health Affairs (Millwood) in 2019, volume 38, issue 11, pages 1824–1831. 63. Lee Y et al. conducted a microsimulation study on the health impact and cost-effectiveness of various sugar-sweetened beverage tax policies in the US, published in Circulation in 2020, volume 142, issue 6, pages 523–534. 64. The USDA provides data on food prices and spending, accessible via their website as of January 1, 2023. 65. A map showing which countries spend the most on food is available on the World Economic Forum website, accessed January 1, 2023. 66. A report on poverty trends in South Africa between 2006 and 2011 is available in PDF format, accessed January 1, 2023.
